questions.question: What is a user in Linux?
questions.answer: A user in Linux is an account that allows someone or something to log into the system and use its resources — access files, run commands, and work with processes. Every user account contains a username, password, UID (unique number), home directory, default shell, and a primary group.

questions.question: What are the three types of users in Linux?
questions.answer: 1. Root user (super user) — UID 0, full administrative privileges, can do anything on the system. 2. Normal user — UID 1000 and above, limited privileges, created by the admin for human use. 3. System user (service account) — UID 1 to 999, created by Linux itself for background services, cannot be used for login.

questions.question: What is the UID of the root user?
questions.answer: The root user always has UID 0. This is the same across every Linux distribution and every system. There is only one root user per system.

questions.question: What is the difference between /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow?
questions.answer: /etc/passwd stores basic information about all user accounts (username, UID, GID, home directory, shell) and is readable by all users. /etc/shadow stores the encrypted (hashed) passwords and is only readable by root. Passwords were separated out for security — /etc/passwd is world-readable, so keeping real passwords there would be a security risk.

questions.question: What does the useradd command do by default?
questions.answer: useradd creates a new user account. By default, it automatically: creates the user with the next available UID (1000+), creates a primary group with the same name as the user, creates a home directory at /home/username, and sets /bin/bash as the default shell.

questions.question: What is the difference between usermod -G and usermod -aG?
questions.answer: usermod -G groupname username REPLACES all secondary group memberships with only the specified group. usermod -aG groupname username APPENDS the new group while keeping all existing groups. Always use -aG to safely add a user to an additional group. Using -G without -a is a common and dangerous mistake.

questions.question: How do you grant sudo access to a user on Amazon Linux?
questions.answer: Add the user to the wheel group: sudo usermod -aG wheel username. On Amazon Linux, CentOS, and RHEL, the wheel group grants sudo access. On Ubuntu and Debian, you would use the sudo group instead: sudo usermod -aG sudo username.

questions.question: What is the purpose of sudo?
questions.answer: sudo (superuser do) lets a normal user run a single command with root privileges without switching to the root account. After the command completes, the user returns to normal privileges. It is safer than logging in as root because the elevated privilege is temporary and limited to one specific command.

questions.question: What command shows a user's UID and group memberships?
questions.answer: The id command: 'id username' shows the user's UID, primary GID, and all groups they belong to. Example output: uid=1001(vikram) gid=1001(vikram) groups=1001(vikram),1002(developers). This is the key command to verify any user or group management change.

questions.question: How do you delete a user and their home directory?
questions.answer: Use userdel -r username. The -r flag removes the home directory along with the account. Without -r, the account is deleted but the home directory at /home/username remains and must be removed manually with: sudo rm -rf /home/username.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you needed to manage user permissions on a Linux server.
questions.answer: (Situation) We had a new developer join the team who needed access to the application's shared codebase on our EC2 server. (Task) I needed to create their account, set a password, and add them to the developers group so they could access the shared files. (Action) I SSH'd into the server, ran sudo useradd newdev, set a password with sudo passwd newdev, then added them to the developers group with sudo usermod -aG developers newdev. I verified with id newdev to confirm the group was showing. (Result) The developer was able to access the shared directory immediately. The whole process took under 5 minutes.

questions.question: A junior admin accidentally ran usermod -G docker username instead of usermod -aG docker username. What happened and how would you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) The -G flag without -a replaces all secondary group memberships. The user lost all their previous secondary groups — like wheel (sudo access), developers, etc. (Task) Restore the correct group memberships without disrupting the user's session. (Action) Check which groups the user should be in from documentation or HR records. Then run: sudo usermod -aG wheel,developers,docker username to restore all groups at once. Verify with id username. (Result) Group memberships restored. This is why -aG is the safe practice and -G alone should almost never be used.

questions.question: Describe how you would set up a new EC2 instance and connect to it via SSH.
questions.answer: (Situation) We needed a new development server. (Task) Launch and connect to a fresh EC2 instance. (Action) 1. In AWS console, launch an EC2 instance (Amazon Linux 2023, t3.micro free tier). 2. Create or select a key pair — the .pem file is the private key. 3. Configure security group to allow SSH on port 22 from my IP. 4. After launch, copy the public IP. 5. On my laptop: cd to the Downloads folder where the .pem file is, then run: ssh -i 'key.pem' ec2-user@PUBLIC_IP. 6. Accept the host fingerprint and the connection succeeds. (Result) Successfully connected as ec2-user in the home directory.

questions.question: How would you check what groups a user belongs to, and what file would you look at to verify?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to audit a user's group memberships. (Task) Check current group memberships and verify. (Action) Run 'id username' for a quick summary showing UID, primary GID, and all groups. For detailed verification, run 'cat /etc/group | grep username' to see all groups where this user is listed as a member. Also check their primary group from /etc/passwd. (Result) Complete picture of the user's group memberships. The id command is fastest for a quick check; /etc/group is best for a full audit.

questions.question: A user forgot their password. How would you reset it as a system administrator?
questions.answer: (Situation) A normal user cannot log in because they forgot their password. (Task) Reset the password as an admin without knowing the old one. (Action) Log in as ec2-user or another sudo-capable account. Run: sudo passwd username. Linux will prompt for a new password twice — no need to know the old one. The new encrypted password is saved to /etc/shadow. (Result) User can now log in with the new password. Note: In production, enforce a policy that users change their password on first login: sudo chage -d 0 username.

questions.question: Someone created a user with useradd but forgot to use -r to remove the home directory when deleting them. How do you clean up?
questions.answer: (Situation) userdel was run without -r, so the account is deleted but /home/username still exists with all its files. (Task) Remove the orphaned home directory. (Action) Check the directory still exists: ls /home/. Then remove it: sudo rm -rf /home/username. The -r flag makes rm recursive (enters directories) and -f forces removal without prompts. Before deleting, consider whether the user's files need to be archived or transferred. (Result) Directory removed, disk space freed.

questions.question: How do you find out which users on the system are normal users versus system users?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to audit all user accounts on a server. (Task) Identify which accounts are human users vs service accounts. (Action) Run: cat /etc/passwd and examine the UID column (3rd field). Any entry with UID 0 is root. UIDs 1–999 are system/service accounts (like sshd, apache, mysql). UIDs 1000 and above are normal users. You can also filter: awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd to list only normal users. (Result) Quick audit of all account types on the system.

questions.question: Why does Linux not require antivirus software the way Windows does?
questions.answer: (Situation) A manager asks why we are not spending on antivirus for our Linux servers. (Task) Explain Linux's built-in security model. (Action) Linux uses a granular file permission system where every file has read, write, and execute permissions set for three levels: the owning user, the owning group, and everyone else. This is enforced at the kernel level for every single operation. Unlike Windows where files can often be executed or modified by default, Linux denies access unless explicitly granted. Additionally, system files are owned by root and protected from modification by normal users. (Result) Linux's permission architecture provides strong baseline security without additional antivirus software.

questions.question: Explain the concept of primary group vs secondary groups with a real-world analogy.
questions.answer: (Situation) Explaining Linux groups to a new team member. (Task) Make the concept intuitive. (Action) Think of it like department membership in a company. Your primary department (primary group) is where you officially belong — when you create documents, they are filed under your department by default. Secondary departments (secondary groups) are other teams you collaborate with. For example, a developer (primary group: developers) might also be in the docker group (to use containers) and the wheel group (for admin tasks). Each group membership grants different access rights. (Result) The person now understands that a user has one home team (primary group) but can be a member of multiple working groups (secondary groups).

questions.question: Describe the SSH key authentication process. Why is it more secure than password authentication?
questions.answer: (Situation) Setting up secure remote access for a team. (Task) Explain SSH key authentication and its advantages. (Action) SSH key authentication works with a key pair: a private key (stored on your laptop, never shared) and a public key (stored in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server). When you connect, the SSH client uses your private key to prove your identity; the server verifies it against the stored public key. No password travels over the network. This is more secure than passwords because: 1) No password can be intercepted, 2) Keys are much longer and harder to brute-force, 3) The private key never leaves your machine. (Result) AWS EC2 uses this method by default for this reason.

questions.question: If a system user account is compromised by an attacker through a vulnerability in that service, why can't the attacker immediately access the entire system?
questions.answer: System users run with limited, isolated privileges — they can only access the files and resources that their specific service needs. For example, the apache user can only read web files in /var/www and write to apache log files. It cannot access /home directories, modify system files, or run privileged commands. This is the principle of least privilege in action. The attacker would be confined to what that service account can do, which is a very small subset of the system. Escalating to root from a service account requires exploiting additional vulnerabilities, which is much harder than if they had already compromised an admin account.

questions.question: What is the sudoers file and why must you use visudo to edit it?
questions.answer: The /etc/sudoers file defines who can use sudo, which commands they can run, and whether a password is required. It is the security policy file for privilege escalation. visudo must be used to edit it because visudo validates the file syntax before saving. A single typo in /etc/sudoers can make the file invalid and lock everyone out of sudo on the system — including the ability to recover it. visudo catches syntax errors before they take effect. It also uses file locking to prevent two admins from editing it simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the security implication of the NOPASSWD:ALL configuration in sudoers, and when is it appropriate?
questions.answer: NOPASSWD:ALL means the user can run any command as root without entering a password. The security implication is that if someone gains access to that user account (through SSH session hijacking, a vulnerable application, or physical access), they immediately have root access without any additional authentication barrier. It is appropriate in controlled scenarios like: EC2 instances accessed only via SSH key pairs (the key itself is the authentication factor), automated deployment pipelines running commands non-interactively, or development/test environments. In production, especially for accounts accessed via password, sudo should always require a password.

questions.question: How does Linux use UIDs internally, and why does this matter for file ownership when a user is deleted?
questions.answer: Linux tracks file ownership using UIDs, not usernames. The username displayed is just a mapping the system looks up in /etc/passwd. If you delete a user without removing their files, the files still show the UID number but the system cannot resolve it to a name — they appear as owned by the raw UID number. If you then create a new user and they happen to get the same UID (1001, for example), that new user will inherit ownership of all the previous user's files. This is a security concern — always remove user files when deleting accounts, especially in multi-tenant environments.

questions.question: Describe the complete architecture of how a Linux user account is stored across the three /etc files.
questions.answer: User account data is spread across three files: /etc/passwd stores the account's basic profile — username, UID, GID (primary group), home directory, and default shell. The password field shows 'x' as a placeholder. /etc/shadow stores the sensitive data — the actual hashed password, password expiry settings, and account expiry. Only root can read this. /etc/group stores group definitions — group name, GID, and list of members. A user's primary group is referenced by GID in /etc/passwd; secondary group memberships are stored as member entries in /etc/group. Together these three files give the complete picture of every user identity and group relationship on the system.
